title: "The Beneficent, the Merciful"
hook: mercy, named twice, before the word judgment ever appears

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rabb, the one who raises and looks after every world. Your line was every world is tended. Which small world did you notice? Day eight.

Picture a horse in a field with her foal pressed close against her legs. She's about to shift her weight, and she stops, lifts one hoof, and holds it in the air, so she won't step on him. Nobody taught her that. There's a hadith that uses exactly that picture. It says that all the tenderness in the world, every mother and every foal, every hand that steadies someone else, comes from one small share of a much greater mercy. Today's verse is two words long, and both of them are that mercy.
screen: `A MARE LIFTS HER HOOF.` → `ONE SHARE OF MERCY.` → `VERSE THREE: TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Pickthall's words: “The Beneficent, the Merciful.” Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. If that sounds familiar, it should. They're the two names from verse one, the doorway, said again. Both come from one root, r-h-m, and the noun is today's word: rahma, mercy. The same root makes rahim, the womb. In this language, mercy has the shape of the place where you were held before you were born. A hadith in Bukhari draws the line straight: the ties of the womb, family, kinship, take their name from ar-Rahman. Why two names? Many scholars explain it like this. Ar-Rahman is mercy as wide as everything, reaching every creature, whoever they are. Ar-Rahim is mercy that stays, that keeps coming back to you in particular. And the hook's picture? A hadith in Muslim's collection says God made mercy in a hundred parts, and sent one part down into the world. With that one part, creatures are gentle with each other, even the mare lifting her hoof from her foal. The other ninety-nine are kept back. Now look at where the verse sits. Praise, then mercy, then mercy again, and only after that, tomorrow, the word judgment. Scholars have long read an order in that. Another well-known hadith, in Bukhari and Muslim, says that when God created the world, He wrote that His mercy outstrips His anger. The prayer is built the same way. In the conversation hadith from yesterday, God answers this verse too: My servant has extolled Me. Three verses down, four to go.
screen: `THE TWO NAMES FROM VERSE ONE.` · `R-H-M — THE ROOT OF WOMB.` · `WIDE MERCY, MERCY THAT STAYS.` · `MERCY OUTSTRIPS ANGER.` · then, large: `MERCY TWICE BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: The bell will give you about forty-five seconds. Sit comfortably. First, the wide mercy: think of something good that reaches everyone, sunlight, rain, the air in this breath. Stay with it. Then the mercy that stays: someone who kept coming back for you, even when you didn't make it easy. Let their face come. If you pray, you can hold the two names: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. If you don't, hold the two pictures. The bell holds the time.
Rahma. Mercy, from the root of the womb, named twice in a row: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. Eighth word.
Your line: mercy twice before anything else. Before you judge anything today, a person, a message, yourself, find two kind things to say about it first. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "OWNER OF THE DAY OF JUDGMENT."`

howItsDone: Muslims say these two names in every unit of every prayer, twice over: in the bismillah and again in verse three. Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim are also among the names of God Muslims call on in their own prayers, and many children are named Abdur-Rahman or Abdur-Rahim, servant of the Merciful.

fork.setup: the hadith in Muslim's collection says God made mercy in a hundred parts. how many were sent into the world?
fork.reveal: one part, and by it every creature is gentle with another, even a mare lifting her hoof from her foal. ninety-nine are kept back.

original.note: Arabic: mercy. from r-h-m, the root of rahim, womb, and of the two names ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim.

trapdoor: what you thought: mercy means letting someone off.
what it means: rahma, a mercy that holds and shelters, like a womb.
what a scholar hears: ar-Rahman (an intensive form, mercy reaching all) and ar-Rahim (mercy that continues) are one root doubled; Bukhari's hadith derives the womb-tie, rahim, from ar-Rahman.
